questions.prompt: The HQ exhibit needs a map. The draft marks an active hornbill nest. What do you send to print?

choices.text: Print a species panel and leave the map out.
choices.justification: The nest stays private. Visitors lose the chance to learn about the wider habitat.

choices.text: Hold the whole exhibit while looking for a different photo.
choices.justification: Waiting avoids disclosure, but a safe map or text panel could open now.

choices.text: Print the active nest marker so visitors can find it.
choices.justification: A public marker makes disturbance at the nest more likely.

choices.text: Print a habitat overview with the nest and access clues removed.
choices.justification: A broad habitat map teaches visitors while keeping the active nest private.

questions.prompt: A school sends a hornbill photo for the noticeboard. The caption and image reveal how to find its nest. What do you post?

choices.text: Ask for a photo with no location clues and use a habitat caption.
choices.justification: Removing identifying clues from both the image and caption helps keep the nest private.

choices.text: Post the original image and caption to credit the class.
choices.justification: Crediting the class does not make the nest clues safe to publish.

choices.text: Leave the photo out and give the class no feedback.
choices.justification: The location stays private, but the class misses a chance to learn how to share safely.

choices.text: Use a text-only note about hornbills.
choices.justification: A general note avoids exposing the nest, with less context for the school's contribution.

questions.prompt: A radio presenter wants a live interview at an active nest. What can the Manager offer?

choices.text: Broadcast from the nest and describe how to reach it.
choices.justification: Public directions expose an active nest to disturbance well beyond the interview.

choices.text: Decline the interview without an explanation.
choices.justification: Declining keeps the location private and leaves a useful public question unanswered.

choices.text: Offer a phone interview about hornbill habitat.
choices.justification: The interview can go ahead without revealing the site, though listeners may still ask why.

choices.text: Record at the visitor centre and explain why nest sites stay private.
choices.justification: A public venue gives the station a story without bringing an audience to the nest.

questions.prompt: A visitor reports an injured wild bird beside a Sarawak park car park. What should the Manager tell them?

choices.text: Ask the visitor to take the bird home and see how it does.
choices.justification: Untrained handling can harm the animal and put the visitor at risk.

choices.text: Write it down for a routine update at the next shift.
choices.justification: A delayed note gives responders less time to assess a potentially injured bird.

choices.text: Keep people back and privately tell park staff what you saw and where.
choices.justification: Staff can assess the report and arrange help while people and the bird keep their distance.

choices.text: Give the visitor directions to the park desk so they can report it.
choices.justification: The desk can help route the report. Guidance for the people already gathering is still needed.

questions.prompt: A reported wildlife injury comes in after the visitor desk closes. No Ranger is there yet. What should the Manager do?

choices.text: Send the caller the visitor desk's opening hours.
choices.justification: Opening hours do not provide a way to get the wildlife report assessed now.

choices.text: Use the official wildlife reporting channel and ask callers to keep clear.
choices.justification: The appropriate team gets a timely report without asking visitors to approach the animal.

choices.text: Refer the caller to the official wildlife reporting channel.
choices.justification: That reaches the appropriate team, though it leaves the caller to pass on the report.

choices.text: Ask the public to gather and move the animal before staff arrive.
choices.justification: A crowd and untrained handling add risks to the animal and bystanders.

questions.prompt: A clip shows a feathered young bird on the ground with no adult in frame. The post calls it abandoned. What do you say?

choices.text: Ask the park team for advice before repeating the claim.
choices.justification: This avoids a premature diagnosis. A public reply could also stop others acting on the clip.

choices.text: Explain that the clip cannot establish abandonment. Refer injury concerns to staff.
choices.justification: A young bird out of its nest can still receive parental care. Qualified staff can assess concerns.

choices.text: Share a general bird photo with no reply to the report.
choices.justification: A general photo does not resolve the concern or help visitors report an injury.

choices.text: Tell viewers to collect any young bird they find alone.
choices.justification: Being alone in a short clip does not establish abandonment. Collection can disrupt care.

questions.prompt: An old flood photo is being shared as proof that today's park entrance is closed. What should Outreach publish?

choices.text: Check the photo date and park notice, then post the confirmed access status.
choices.justification: Date and source checks distinguish an old image from a current closure.

choices.text: Share the photo as a current closure notice.
choices.justification: Passing on an unverified old photo can misdirect visitors.

choices.text: Post that weather can affect access, with no update on the entrance.
choices.justification: The statement is true but leaves the claim and the access question unresolved.

choices.text: Link the park's current access notice and omit the photo.
choices.justification: Visitors get a current source. A short correction would also explain the misleading image.

questions.prompt: A forwarded message names a village as responsible for wildlife theft. No report verifies it. What goes in the public update?

choices.text: Post a general conservation slogan and leave the claim unanswered.
choices.justification: The post avoids amplifying the claim, but does not tell readers what can be verified.

choices.text: Name the village in a warning as if the accusation were confirmed.
choices.justification: An unsupported accusation can harm residents and mislead the public.

choices.text: Say the claim is unverified and direct readers to official updates.
choices.justification: This limits repetition. Passing the underlying tip to the right staff would help check it.

choices.text: State what staff have verified and send the tip privately for assessment.
choices.justification: A private report keeps an unverified accusation out of the public statement and permits follow-up.

questions.prompt: HQ publicly shared last month's trail notice by mistake. What should the Manager do after confirming the current notice?

choices.text: Delete the old post and leave the page without an update.
choices.justification: Deletion stops fresh views of the error but gives visitors no current access information.

choices.text: Replace the poster with a link to the confirmed notice.
choices.justification: The HQ page is now accurate. People who saw the original may miss the change.

choices.text: Publish a dated correction and share the confirmed notice where the error spread.
choices.justification: People who saw the first update can see both the correction and its verified source.

choices.text: Keep sharing the old notice with the date cropped out.
choices.justification: Removing context makes the stale information easier to mistake for a current notice.

questions.prompt: A supporter asks how many saplings the weekend appeal funded. Some are ordered and others are planted. What do you report?

choices.text: Share the confirmed planting count and promise an update on orders.
choices.justification: The published planting figure is reliable. The order status remains to be explained.

choices.text: Share verified figures and label ordered and planted saplings separately.
choices.justification: Separate counts let supporters see what has happened and what is still pending.

choices.text: Send a thank-you with no progress figures.
choices.justification: The reply acknowledges support but leaves a straightforward accountability question open.

choices.text: Report ordered and planted saplings together as already planted.
choices.justification: That gives supporters a false count of completed work.

questions.prompt: Donations were requested for seedling supplies. HQ now wants to use part for event banners. What should Outreach say?

choices.text: Explain that the gift stays with seedlings and seek separate banner funds.
choices.justification: The reply tells supporters where the gift goes and gives HQ a separate way to fund the banners.

choices.text: Keep the seedling funds separate and seek other funding for banners.
choices.justification: This respects the appeal. A clear update would help supporters follow what happened.

choices.text: Buy the banners with the gift and keep reporting seedling spending.
choices.justification: Spending and reporting against different purposes misleads the people who gave.

choices.text: Postpone the discussion and leave supporters without an update.
choices.justification: The funds are left untouched, but the purpose and next steps stay unclear.

questions.prompt: A sponsor pledges funds for restoration. The transfer is still pending. How should a public progress report describe it?

choices.text: Report only confirmed receipts and update after the transfer.
choices.justification: The report stays accurate with less context about the pending pledge.

choices.text: Label the amount as pledged and show confirmed receipts separately.
choices.justification: Pledges and funds already received are different stages and visitors can see both.

choices.text: Leave out all figures until next month.
choices.justification: This avoids overstating receipts but withholds confirmed progress the team could share.

choices.text: Include the pledge in the money already received.
choices.justification: The report would overstate the amount of funds available.

questions.prompt: A proposed clean-up clashes with a nearby community's market morning. How should the Manager arrange the volunteer day?

choices.text: Reduce the volunteer group but keep the conflicting time.
choices.justification: A smaller turnout may help, but the schedule conflict and access needs remain.

choices.text: Postpone and ask residents for times that would work.
choices.justification: Residents can give input, though park staffing and access still need to be coordinated.

choices.text: Keep the booking and tell volunteers to take over market access.
choices.justification: The event would disrupt the people who rely on that access.

choices.text: Ask market organisers and park staff to agree on a suitable time and access plan.
choices.justification: Both groups can describe their needs before Outreach commits volunteers to a schedule.

questions.prompt: Residents explain a local conservation practice at a meeting. The team wants to feature their account. What happens before publication?

choices.text: Share general conservation advice without using the residents' account.
choices.justification: This respects the unreleased account. A future agreed version could give the community a voice.

choices.text: Ask what can be shared and let contributors check how their account is presented.
choices.justification: The people who shared the knowledge can decide what to make public and correct misunderstandings.

choices.text: Leave the idea out without following up with contributors.
choices.justification: Their account stays private, but contributors get no say in a potential joint feature.

choices.text: Print the private discussion and claim the meeting granted permission.
choices.justification: Attending a discussion does not establish consent to publish what participants shared.

questions.prompt: A field trip wants to pass through a village during a local event. The guide has no agreement from residents. What should Outreach arrange?

choices.text: Promise the group access through the village without checking permission.
choices.justification: The promise puts pressure on residents who have made no agreement.

choices.text: Choose an approved public route clear of the event.
choices.justification: This protects the event and offers visitors a workable outing with less shared planning.

choices.text: Ask local organisers about access and agree on an alternative if needed.
choices.justification: People hosting the event can explain what access works before visitors arrive.

choices.text: Cancel the visit without seeking another date or route.
choices.justification: Cancellation avoids a conflict but misses a chance to arrange a suitable visit.

questions.prompt: Visitors want to leave snacks so wildlife comes closer for a family photo. What should the Manager offer?

choices.text: Explain why feeding is harmful and suggest watching quietly from a distance.
choices.justification: Visitors can see natural behaviour and avoid drawing animals toward people or human food.

choices.text: Remind the group to keep food packed away.
choices.justification: That prevents feeding. A safe observation option would also answer the photo request.

choices.text: Let the group feed wildlife to get the photograph.
choices.justification: Feeding encourages wild animals to approach people and can harm the animals.

choices.text: Move on to the next activity without answering their request.
choices.justification: Changing the subject leaves the group with no guidance about trying it later.

questions.prompt: A tour operator asks HQ to promise a close-up encounter with nesting hornbills. What should the booking description say?

choices.text: Decline the close-up request and share the park's birdwatching guidance.
choices.justification: The guidance protects the birds, though the operator has no replacement activity yet.

choices.text: List a birdwatching trip without addressing the close-up request.
choices.justification: The listing avoids a promise, but the operator may still expect close access.

choices.text: Advertise a guaranteed close approach to nesting birds.
choices.justification: A guaranteed close encounter pressures the guide to disturb the birds.

choices.text: Offer a quiet habitat walk and explain that close encounters are never promised.
choices.justification: The tour sets realistic expectations and protects birds from pressure around active nests.

questions.prompt: A picnic group leaves food scraps at a lookout so animals can eat them. What should Outreach tell the group?

choices.text: Ask them to pack out leftovers and explain that scraps attract wildlife to visitors.
choices.justification: Taking scraps away keeps food out of reach and reduces wildlife attraction to busy areas.

choices.text: Remind them only to collect their plastic wrappers.
choices.justification: Removing wrappers helps, but edible leftovers can still draw wildlife toward people.

choices.text: Ask the group to take all their rubbish and leftovers away.
choices.justification: It addresses the scraps. Explaining the wildlife risk may help the group remember next time.

choices.text: Tell the group that leaving edible leftovers helps wild animals.
choices.justification: Leftover food encourages wildlife to seek food around people.

questions.prompt: Park staff close a trail after a storm. A visitor asks HQ to suggest a shortcut around the closure. What should you offer?

choices.text: Recommend leaving the trail to get around the closed section.
choices.justification: That bypasses the park's safety decision and can damage habitat off the path.

choices.text: Share only a general park map with no current access notes.
choices.justification: The map does not answer which route is open today.

choices.text: Confirm an open route with staff and post the closure alongside it.
choices.justification: Visitors get a usable option that respects the closure and keeps them on authorised paths.

choices.text: Ask visitors to keep the closure and check with the park desk.
choices.justification: The closure is respected. A confirmed alternative would be easier for visitors to use.

questions.prompt: A student group arrives at a route reserved for park work. The approved visitor path is open. How should the Manager redirect them?

choices.text: Post the activity time again without giving an entry point.
choices.justification: The update gives the group no way to choose the correct route.

choices.text: Let the group enter the work route while staff are busy.
choices.justification: Unauthorised access can interrupt park work and expose visitors to hazards.

choices.text: Explain the restriction and start the activity from the approved visitor path.
choices.justification: The group can still participate while respecting the park team's work and the route restriction.

choices.text: Ask the group to return to the park desk for route guidance.
choices.justification: Staff can redirect them safely, with a delay to the activity.
